C343 · Costa Rica · 2008 · 10 colones · CRC

payload.story: A Costa Rican 10 colones from 2008, struck in feather-light aluminium. One side carries the national arms: seven stars for the seven provinces, three volcanoes, a sunrise, and the sea on either side for the two oceans Costa Rica sits between. The other side states the value twice over, once in big numerals and once in Braille dots under the word COLONES, so the coin can be read by touch. These aluminium pieces were everyday small change by the hundreds of millions; Costa Rica later switched the denomination to stainless steel to cut costs.

items_full.label: C344 · Japan · Heisei 14 (2002) · 10 yen · JPY

payload.story: A Japanese 10 yen in bronze, dated Heisei 14 (2002), the fourteenth year of Emperor Akihito's reign. One side shows the Phoenix Hall of Byodoin temple in Uji, a thousand-year-old building so loved that it also appears on the 10,000 yen note. The other side frames a big 10 in a wreath of evergreen leaves. Japan has struck this design, nearly unchanged, since 1951, and it is still the 10 yen in everyday pockets today. The collection already holds two Showa-era strikes of the same design from 1982 and 1988; this is its first Heisei one.

record.mint: Japan Mint (no mint mark on this type)

items_full.label: C345 · Australia · 2008 · 10 cents · AUD

payload.story: An Australian 10 cents from 2008, the everyday silver coin with the superb lyrebird fanning its tail across the back — the bird that can mimic almost any sound it hears, drawn here feather by feather. The front carries Queen Elizabeth the Second in Ian Rank-Broadley's portrait, the one Australia used from the late 1990s until the Queen's death. The lyrebird design by Stuart Devlin has been on the 10 cents since decimal currency began in 1966. The collection already holds a 2006 strike of this same coin; this 2008 joins it as a second year.

record.metal: copper-nickel (75% copper, 25% nickel) · 5.66 g · 23.6 mm · Reeded
record.design: obverse 4th portrait bust of Elizabeth II right wearing tiara · ELIZABETH II AUSTRALIA · reverse superb lyrebird displaying plumage · 10 · Stuart Devlin / Ian Rank-Broadley

items_full.label: C346 · Mexico · 1975 · 1 peso · MXP

payload.story: A Mexican one peso from 1975, carrying Jose Maria Morelos, the priest who became a general of Mexico's independence war and was executed for it in 1815. His portrait faces left under the words UN PESO; the other side shows Mexico's national emblem, the eagle with a snake in its beak standing on a cactus — the sign the Aztecs were told to look for when founding their city. Mexico struck this peso, in copper-nickel, through the 1970s and into the early 1980s, and it jingled in every pocket and bus fare in the country. The little Mo beside the portrait is the Mexico City mint's mark, one of the oldest mints in the Americas.

items_full.label: C347 · Guernsey · 1893 · 8 doubles · GGP

payload.story: Eight doubles from Guernsey, dated 1893 — the oldest coin in this batch, struck while Queen Victoria was on the throne, though Guernsey's coins show no portrait: just the island's shield with its three lions, inherited from the island's Norman past, and a sprig of leaves. The double was Guernsey's own money, a Channel Islands coinage counted eight to a British penny, and this big bronze piece is the penny-sized one — Guernsey kept its doubles for a century before joining the pound in full. It is the collection's first coin from Guernsey. This one has lived a life: dark, worn smooth in places, with pale corrosion spots on the shield side.

record.mint: no mint mark read — the area below the date is too dark in the photos to call

items_full.label: C348 · East Caribbean States · 2004 · 10 cents · XCD

payload.story: Ten cents from the East Caribbean States, dated 2004 — pocket money shared by eight Caribbean islands under one dollar and one central bank. The ship is the Golden Hind, the galleon Sir Francis Drake sailed around the world in the 1570s, drawn by Thomas Humphrey Paget; the crowned portrait of Queen Elizabeth the Second on the front is by Ian Rank-Broadley. This is the copper-nickel striking the islands used before switching to lighter steel coins in 2009, made for them at the Royal Mint in Britain. The collection already holds a 2004 strike of this coin recorded earlier from a shorthand note; this is the first one photographed on both sides.

record.mint: Royal Mint (United Kingdom); no mint mark on this issue; date on the ship side
record.design: obverse Elizabeth II · reverse Golden Hind under sail · EAST CARIBBEAN STATES · 10 flanking masts · TEN CENTS

items_full.label: C349 · Australia · 1977 · 50 cents · AUD

payload.story: An Australian 50 cents from 1977, struck for Queen Elizabeth the Second's Silver Jubilee — twenty-five years on the throne. It is a big twelve-sided coin. The front shows the young Queen in Arnold Machin's famous portrait, the one Australia used through the sixties and seventies. The back is a celebration wreath: a shining starburst in the middle ringed by small emblems, with the words SILVER JUBILEE and 50 CENTS around them. It was designed by Stuart Devlin, the goldsmith behind most of Australia's first decimal coins, and it was made to be kept — but plenty slipped into change anyway.

record.mint: Royal Australian Mint (Canberra); no mint mark on this issue

items_full.label: C350 · East Caribbean States · 1991 · 10 cents · XCD

payload.story: Ten cents from the East Caribbean States, dated 1991 — an older brother to the 2004 ten cents filed the same day (C348). The back is the same Golden Hind, Drake's little round-the-world galleon, with a 10 on each side. The front is what gives its age away: the Queen is young here, in Arnold Machin's portrait wearing a tiara, the likeness these islands used from the 1980s into the early 2000s before switching to the older crowned portrait. Eight Caribbean islands spend this one money, and coins like this crossed between them in every ferry and market stall. This one is copper-nickel, from the British Royal Mint years, heavier in the hand than the steel strikes that replaced it.

record.mint: Royal Mint (United Kingdom); no mint mark on this issue

items_full.label: C351 · France · 1867 · 10 centimes · FRF

payload.story: A big bronze ten centimes from the France of Napoleon the Third, dated 1867 — three years before his empire collapsed in the Franco-Prussian War. One side carries the Emperor's head wreathed in laurel, ringed by his name and title; the other shows the imperial eagle standing on a thunderbolt, the emblem Napoleon's regiments had carried into battle, with EMPIRE FRANCAIS above and DIX CENTIMES below between two stars. These heavy bronze pieces were the workhorse small change of France for decades — struck in the tens of millions, they stayed in pockets and tills into the next century, which is why so many survive as worn as this one.

record.mint: mint letter below the eagle's thunderbolt not readable in the photos

items_full.label: C352 · Mexico · 1943 · 20 centavos · MXP

payload.story: One of Mexico's best-loved coin designs, struck in bronze from 1943: the Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan fills the reverse, its name carved at the pyramid's base, with the twin volcanoes Iztaccihuatl and Popocatepetl smoking behind it and a radiant Liberty cap dividing the big 20 overhead. Mexico authorized the type in August 1943, in the middle of the Second World War, to replace the silver twenty centavos it could no longer afford to strike - this is a first-year piece, one of some 46 million poured out that year. The obverse carries the national arms, the eagle on its cactus with the snake, and the words ESTADOS UNIDOS MEXICANOS.

record.mint: Mexico City (Mo, below the radiant cap on the reverse)

items_full.label: C353 · Japan · Heisei 8 (1996) · 10 yen · JPY

payload.story: A Heisei-era ten yen piece, dated in the eighth year of Emperor Akihito's reign - 1996. The obverse shows the Phoenix Hall of Byodo-in temple at Uji, its wing-like roofs spread over the water it was built beside in 1053; the reverse carries the big 10 inside an evergreen-oak wreath, with the era date written out in kanji below. The same design has been on Japan's ten yen since 1959 and still circulates today; this one joins the Heisei 14 (2002) specimen filed from a chat photo the same day.

record.mint: Japan Mint; no mint mark (Japanese coinage carries none)

items_full.label: C354 · India · 2014 · 2 rupees · INR

payload.story: A two rupees from the India of 2014, part of the series launched in 2011 to carry the rupee's new symbol - the sign that blends the Latin R with the Devanagari RA, adopted in 2010 to give the currency a mark of its own like the dollar or the pound. It sits above the big 2, with lotus flowers curling up both sides. The other face carries the Lion Capital of Ashoka, the four lions of the emperor's pillar that India took as its state emblem, with the country's name in Hindi on the left and English on the right and the motto Truth Alone Triumphs beneath. The small dot under the date marks it as a product of the Noida mint, outside Delhi.
